parts.objective: Identify the three types of tracked objects and the four stages of operation

key_points.text: Broadly, three things can be tracked: the user's sense organs, the user's other body parts, and the external environment.
Trackers are categorized into two types: inside-out and outside-in.
Inside-out trackers place all sensors on the device used by the user, while outside-in trackers place sensors in the surrounding environment.
Key point: The overall tracking process involves four stages: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. (cited sentences)

terms.name: Tracking
terms.definition: Tracking is a process that involves understanding how trackers work through four distinct stages: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

terms.name: Tracking process
terms.definition: The tracking process describes how tracking is performed and consists of three distinct components, including understanding how the trackers work.

terms.name: Inside-out
terms.definition: Inside-out is a type of tracker where all the necessary sensors are placed on the device that the user is using.

terms.name: Outside-in
terms.definition: Outside-in is a type of tracker that utilizes sensors placed in the surrounding environment rather than on the device being used by the user.

terms.name: Calibration
terms.definition: Calibration is one of the four primary stages in the overall tracking process.

terms.name: Registration
terms.definition: Registration is one of the four primary stages in the overall tracking process.

terms.name: Integration

parts.objective: Identify and describe the components and function of Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) in tracking systems

key_points.text: IMU stands for Inertial Measurement Unit, which is a composite hardware containing three main sensor types.
An IMU typically comprises a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer.
The gyroscope captures angular velocity, while the accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the three axes.
Tracking with an IMU sensor primarily relies on gyroscopic readings (angular velocity), while accelerometer and magnetometer readings help detect drift.

terms.name: Inertial measurement unit
terms.definition: The Inertial Measurement Unit is a composite piece of hardware that includes a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer. It is commonly found in modern devices like mobile phones and head-mounted displays.

terms.name: Gyroscope
terms.definition: A gyroscope is a sensor that specifically captures angular velocity. When used in IMU tracking, it relies heavily on its readings to estimate position and movement.

terms.name: Accelerometer
terms.definition: Accelerometer is a sensor that captures linear acceleration along the three axes (x, y, and z). While it does not directly contribute to tracking estimation, it is used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

terms.name: Magnetometer
terms.definition: Magnetometer is a sensor that captures magnetic field strength along the three axes. While it does not directly contribute to tracking estimation, it is used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

parts.objective: Explain the process of calibrating imperfect sensor data by mathematically modeling and correcting measurement errors

key_points.text: Imperfect sensors lead to measurement error, defined as the difference between the measured angular velocity (omega g) and the actual angular velocity (omega a) (S46, S47).
Calibration often proposes a linear relationship between the measured and actual velocities, such as omega g = a + b * omega a (S52).
Calibration requires collecting many samples from inexpensive, inaccurate sensors and highly accurate benchmark sensors (S60, S64).
The parameters used for calibration are determined by optimizing the expression, which is a classical regression problem called linear least squares (S70, S72).

terms.name: Calibration
terms.definition: Calibration is the stage where mathematical corrections are applied to imperfect sensor readings to make them as close as possible to the ideal or actual values.

terms.name: Gyroscope
terms.definition: A gyroscope is a device that provides a measurement of angular velocity.

terms.name: Angular velocity
terms.definition: Angular velocity is a value captured in the form of numbers from a gyroscope that can be represented as either an actual value or a measured value.

terms.name: Measurement error
terms.definition: Measurement error is the difference that occurs between the measured angular velocity from the sensor and the actual angular velocity.

terms.name: Linear relationship
terms.definition: A linear relationship is a method proposed to relate two values, such as the measured velocity and the actual velocity, using an equation like omega g is a plus b into omega a.

terms.name: IMU sensor
terms.definition: IMU sensor is a type of cheap or inaccurate sensor that is assumed to be used during the calibration process.

terms.name: Benchmark data set
terms.definition: A benchmark data set is a highly accurate reference dataset used during calibration to compare and correct the values obtained from cheaper, inaccurate sensors.

terms.name: Sum of squared errors
terms.definition: The sum of squared errors is a comparison approach where the differences between pairs of samples are computed, squared, and then summed up across all available samples.

terms.name: Regression problem
terms.definition: A regression problem is a mathematical method used to find constants, such as C1 and C2, that optimize or minimize a function, such as the square term of the measurement error.

terms.name: Linear least squares
terms.definition: Linear least squares is a specific type of classical regression problem that is utilized to optimize the expression related to measurement error.

terms.name: Calibrated value
terms.definition: The calibrated value is the corrected output derived from the cheap sensor reading by applying a mathematical transformation to map it close to the expensive sensor output or the real value.

parts.objective: Explain the steps of registration and integration for setting initial alignment and tracking orientation

key_points.text: Registration establishes the initial pose (orientation) of the sensor or user by setting the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds (84, 85).
Fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags significantly aid the registration process, although computer vision techniques can be used without them (89, 90, 91).
The current orientation at time $t$ is computed by integrating the angular velocity samples starting from the initial orientation, represented as the sum of changes over time (98, 103).
Integration involves summing up changes in orientation (change in orientation = angular velocity sample × sampling interval) from the start time to the current time (101, 102, 103).

terms.name: Registration
terms.definition: Registration is the process of determining the initial pose or orientation of a sensor. It sets the initial alignment between the real world and the virtual world.

terms.name: Initial pose
terms.definition: The initial pose is the starting orientation of the sensor or user when the tracking system is turned on. This orientation is used to establish the alignment at the beginning of the tracking process.

terms.surface: fiducial markers or reflectors or tags
terms.name: Fiducial marker
terms.definition: Fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags are objects that can significantly aid the registration process.

terms.name: Computer vision technique
terms.definition: Computer vision techniques are methods that allow registration to be performed even if physical aids like fiducial markers are not present.

terms.name: Integration
terms.definition: Integration is the process of computing the current orientation or pose by summing up all the changes in orientation (from angular velocity samples) starting from the initial orientation.

terms.name: Sampling interval
terms.definition: The sampling interval (delta t) is the regular discrete interval at which the data stream from the sensor arrives.

terms.name: Gyroscopic sensor
terms.definition: A gyroscopic sensor is the sensor that provides the angular velocity samples used to track rotation and change in orientation.

terms.name: Calibrated angular velocity sample
terms.definition: A calibrated angular velocity sample (W cal i) is the specific angular velocity sample obtained at a given instant from the gyroscopic sensor.

parts.objective: Apply techniques, such as blending sensor values using a gain parameter, to correct drift errors in orientation estimation

key_points.text: Drift correction compensates for estimation errors between real and actual values.
For IMU systems, drift correction can be achieved by blending gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer readings.
Sensor data is blended using an expression that incorporates a gain parameter (alpha), a normalized value between 0 and 1.

terms.name: Drift correction
terms.definition: Drift correction is a process that compensates for errors in estimation between the real and actual value, and it is usually achieved by using the help of extra sensors.

terms.name: Gyroscope
terms.definition: The gyroscope is a sensor whose values are integrated to obtain orientation at a given instant.

terms.name: Camera
terms.definition: A camera is an example of an extra sensor that can be utilized in the process of drift correction.

terms.name: IMU
terms.definition: The IMU is a sensor system that can use accelerometer and magnetometer readings, along with gyroscope values, for drift correction.

terms.name: Accelerometer
terms.definition: The accelerometer is a sensor that can be used in conjunction with other sensors to aid in drift correction.

terms.name: Magnetometer
terms.definition: The magnetometer is a sensor that can be used in conjunction with other sensors to aid in drift correction.

terms.name: Gain parameter
terms.definition: The gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used to combine individually computed orientations when correcting for drift.

parts.objective: Describe how virtual reality tracking systems function through the phases of calibration, registration, and drift correction

key_points.text: Calibration transforms data from inexpensive sensors into values comparable to highly accurate sensors using mathematical manipulation.
Registration is the phase where the initial position and orientation of tracked bodies or objects are set.
Drift correction requires at least two sensors to combine separately estimated orientations, often using a gain parameter between 0 and 1.

terms.name: Calibration
terms.definition: Calibration is the process of obtaining sensory values as close as possible, often by using cheap sensors and then applying mathematical manipulation to transform those values to match those from highly accurate sensors.

terms.name: Registration
terms.definition: Registration is the phase where the initial position and orientation of tracked body parts or objects are established, based on the assumed current position and orientation of the sensor.

terms.name: Drift correction
terms.definition: Drift correction is a stage that assumes access to multiple sensors, where the orientation computed separately by those sensors at the same time instant is combined to get a corrected orientation.

terms.name: Gain parameter
terms.definition: Gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 to 1 used to combine separately estimated orientations at a specific time instant to get the drift-corrected orientation.
